doc.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003

title: Alcohol and drugs overblown; his father's worry about jazz clubs; his parents
summary: He thinks the drugs narrative is exaggerated, recalls telling his father why he wanted to play jazz, and describes his long-lived family and his father's work.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Was there ever lessons learned of things not to do?

Oh yes. You know a lot has been written about alcohol and drugs in the jazz community. And I really feel that it has been overblown. And I sometimes wonder whether or not it’s been used early on to kind of discredit the importance of jazz as an art form. Because that

was some of the stuff that early people say oh that music was born in the brothels and houses of ill repute. And it’s funny because when I first started saying I wanted to play jazz I told my father that I wanted to play jazz, because he liked that I was playing the violin, and he said, “Oh I don’t particularly like the idea of you playing jazz because you’ll be in those clubs where all those people are drinking and this, that and the other.” I said, “Daddy, that’s not why I want to play jazz. Because this is a music that I love. That may be a venue of where I have an opportunity to present myself as a musician. But that’s not why I want to get involved in it. I’m not interested in the fast life per se, you know, wine, women and song.” I mean I had a certain amount of that and it was fun but I never allowed myself to get carried away with all of it. I’m not any saint by any — I mean I had my times that I acted young and foolish. But thank God my mother always gave me a sense of entertaining logic 101. And to maintain a balance. My mother is still alive. She is — what is she, 88 now. And she is just as spry and spunky. She would come in here and she would get up and start dancing. She is amazing. And my uncle, her oldest brother, is still alive, he’s 94 years old and lives in Chicago and still drives his car around Chicago. Now if you can drive in Chicago, even at 23, you’re doing something you know what I mean? I wouldn’t get on that Dan Ryan Express. But I come from a line of long livers. My dad unfortunately passed a couple of years ago. He was 90 years old. But he lived a full life and he was a good man. And the thing that was so beautiful about my father is that when we went to the funeral there were so many people. The church was packed. I didn’t realize all these people loved my father. Because my father was a very humble, giving man. A very bright man who unfortunately, because of the racism and segregation did not get an opportunity to exercise his true talents. He was an excellent mechanical drawing — he had impeccable skills. He went to Butler University and studied mechanical drafting. But he couldn’t get a job. He got a job in the plants during the war at Allison Motor Company, you know they make the engines for the airplanes.
